facts.fact: Koi are an ornamental variety of the common carp, Cyprinus carpio var. koi.
A review gives the optimum water temperature for koi as 23–25 °C, the acceptable range as 15–35 °C, and below 12 °C or above 35 °C as critical.
The same review gives pH 7–7.5 as optimum for koi and 7–9.5 as acceptable.
The review gives dissolved oxygen of 5–7 mg/L as optimum for koi and lists below 5 mg/L as critical.
The review gives ammonia of 0–0.025 mg/L as optimum for koi and above 0.3 mg/L as critical; for nitrite, below 0.02 mg/L is optimum and above 0.2 mg/L is critical.
The review reports an aquarium stocking of about 45 young koi per 150 L (0.3 fish/L), and notes that higher density lowers growth, weight gain and survival.
In high-density koi ponds, replacing about 20% of the water daily improved survival of young fish, according to the review.
A typical koi feed contains 31–33% protein, 4–6% fat, 3–5% fiber and 9–10% moisture, according to the review.
The review says koi are typically fed twice a day.
Overfeeding koi raises turbidity and ammonia and can cause oxidative stress.
Feed additives studied for koi colour include about 20% pumpkin meal, 10% red dragon fruit peel meal, or an astaxanthin-related additive at 250 mg per kg of feed.
Protein is the most important and most expensive part of a fish feed, and koi need 10 essential amino acids that they cannot make themselves.
Too little protein slows koi growth. Excess protein is burned for energy, which is more expensive than getting that energy from fat.
The crude protein percentage alone does not show a feed's quality; how well the fish digest the protein matters (Carl D. Webster, Kentucky State University, via Koi Club of San Diego).
Marine fish meal is the highest-quality protein source in fish feeds. Feather meal is high in protein but poorly digested unless it is hydrolyzed.
Koi Club of San Diego feeding schedule: do not feed below 50°F.
Koi Club of San Diego: at 50–65°F feed a cold-weather wheat germ food, starting at 1–2 times a week at 50°F and rising to twice daily by 60°F.
Koi Club of San Diego: at 66–85°F feed a staple, growth or colour food in small portions, 3–6 times daily.
Koi Club of San Diego: above 85°F cut feeding to 1–2 times daily, and the cold-weather formula can be used again because it is easier to digest.
Koi Club of San Diego: above 90°F do not feed at all, because uneaten food adds to the organic load and to oxygen depletion.
Hikari Wheat-Germ label: at 64–86°F (18–30°C) feed 2–4 times a day, giving only what the fish finish within five minutes.
Hikari Wheat-Germ label: at 41–64°F (5–18°C) feed no more than twice daily, preferably during the warmer part of the day.
Hikari Wheat-Germ label: do not feed below 41°F (5°C).
Hikari says to adjust the amount and frequency of feeding to water temperature, water quality, the number and size of fish and their activity, and to remove uneaten food.
Hikari notes that koi may eat much less when they have lost appetite, are ill or are being medicated, so feeding should be watched closely then.
Hikari N-20 can be fed from 60°F (15°C) upward, and 2–4 times daily when water stays above 70°F (21°C).
Hikari warns that koi keep eating even when they are full, so uneaten food should be removed to avoid overfeeding and water-quality problems.
Hikari says pond water in warm climates often stays above 82°F (28°C), and koi digestion slows as the water nears that point.
Hikari: at 68–78°F (20–26°C) feed higher-protein diets 2–4 times daily; above 82°F switch to wheat-germ or multi-season diets.
Hikari: in summer, feed small amounts often and remove food that is not eaten within 3–5 minutes.
Hikari advises feeding koi between 10:00 AM and 4:00 PM and avoiding the 2 hours after sunrise and before sunset.
Warm water holds less oxygen, so Hikari recommends adding aeration with waterfalls, fountains or air pumps in summer.
Hikari suggests using water lilies or shade sails to lower pond temperature and reduce algae, with plant coverage around 30–50%.
Hikari recommends weekly 10–20% water changes with dechlorinated water, and weekly tests of pH, ammonia, nitrite and nitrate.
Koi Club of San Diego says female koi usually mature at about 3 years, though some have bred at 2.
Koi Club of San Diego says spawning chases generally begin when the water reaches about 72°F.
In spring, females swell with eggs and males start chasing them as the water warms.
Koi spawning can last up to two weeks, or stop for a few days and resume the following week.
Koi eggs stick to rocks, plants or the pond liner. Hobbyists collect them on breeding mats, clean mops and brushes.
Parent koi eat many of their eggs, so breeders isolate pairs and remove the parents after spawning.
Koi eggs that turn white have been killed by fungus.
Koi fry hatch in about 3–4 days, according to Koi Club of San Diego.
Koi fry show colour within about a week and keep changing colour for their first 2–3 years.
Crowded ponds or too many males can cause spawning injuries and deaths in koi.
To avoid unwanted spawning, Koi Club of San Diego advises keeping only same-sex koi together, and planning homes for offspring that may grow to 36 inches.
The review reports a male-to-female ratio of about 3:2 for koi breeding, with hatching rates of up to 80% in the cited studies.
Ripe broodstock can be checked by gentle abdominal pressure: males release milky-white sperm and females release yellow eggs.
Koi sex is hard to tell before about 5 months of age or 20–30 cm length, according to the review.
Koi breeders cull fry heavily. The review gives culling of 60–65% of Kohaku at 40 days and 75–80% of Sanke at 25–30 days, with selection continuing to about 6 months.
A Vietnamese shop calls koi spawning media 'giá thể', including aquatic plants, water hyacinth (lục bình), 'chổi đẻ cá chuyên dụng' (spawning brushes) and soft netting.
Vietnamese terms for koi breeding include 'cá bố mẹ' (broodstock), 'bể đẻ' (spawning tank) and 'cá bột' (fry).
Koi food brands named as common on the Vietnamese market include Omega, Aqua Master and Sakura.
Vietnamese pellet food names include 'cám tăng trưởng' (growth food), 'cám tăng màu' (colour food) and 'cám cân bằng dinh dưỡng' (balanced food).
Vietnamese keepers use 'thức ăn lên màu' for colour-enhancing food, 'thức ăn tăng trưởng' for growth food such as Hi-Growth, and 'trùn quế' for earthworms fed to koi.
